concepts.title: SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013: Registration
concepts.description: SEBI notified the Investment Advisers Regulations in January 2013 to bring the activity of giving investment advice under a formal licence. Anyone who proposes to provide investment advice, as defined, must obtain a certificate of registration from SEBI before continuing that activity. The certificate is valid for five years from issue, and an adviser must apply for renewal three months before it expires; existing advisers were given a six-month window to apply when the rules came into force.
misconceptions: Thinking the registration is issued by AMFI rather than SEBI
Believing the certificate is permanent rather than five years
Assuming renewal can be sought after expiry rather than three months before

objectives.text: State who must register as an investment adviser and with which regulator
Recall the validity period and renewal timeline of the registration certificate

AMFI

options.text: RBI

options.text: PFRDA
options.misconception: Confusing the pension regulator with the securities regulator

questions.explanation: The Investment Advisers Regulations require registration with SEBI, the securities market regulator. AMFI is an industry association, RBI regulates banking, and PFRDA regulates pensions, none of which issue the investment adviser certificate.

options.misconception: Confusing the validity with the capital-adequacy compliance window

options.text: Ten years from the date of issue

questions.explanation: The certificate is valid for five years from the date of issue. One year is the period existing advisers had to meet capital-adequacy norms, and ten years is the PMLA record-keeping period, not the certificate validity.

questions.stem: When must an investment adviser apply for renewal of the registration certificate?

options.text: Three months before the expiry of the original certificate
Any time after the certificate has already expired

questions.explanation: Renewal must be applied for three months before the original certificate expires. The six-month window was the one-time period given to existing advisers to apply for certification, not the renewal rule.

concepts.title: Exemptions from Investment Adviser Registration
concepts.description: Not everyone who mentions investments needs an adviser licence. The regulations exempt several categories, including those who only give general comments on economic or market trends without being stock- or product-specific, insurance agents advising solely on insurance products, pension advisers dealing only in pension products, and mutual fund distributors whose advice is merely incidental to distribution. Professionals such as advocates, solicitors and chartered accountants practising their profession are also outside the registration net.
misconceptions: Thinking a mutual fund distributor who advises incidentally must register
Believing an adviser who charges a separate fee is exempt
Assuming general market commentators need registration

objectives.text: Identify who is exempt from the investment adviser registration requirement
Distinguish incidental advice from fee-charging advice that triggers registration

questions.stem: Which of the following persons is required to comply with the registration requirement under the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013?

options.text: An independent financial adviser who charges advisory fees to investors
A mutual fund distributor who only receives commission from the AMC
options.misconception: Overlooking that distributor commission with incidental advice is exempt

options.text: A chartered accountant practising his profession
options.misconception: Ignoring the exemption for practising professionals

options.text: A person who only gives general comments on economic trends
options.misconception: Ignoring the exemption for non-specific general commentary

questions.explanation: An adviser who charges advisory fees to investors is providing investment advice as a business and must register. A distributor earning only commission (advice incidental to distribution), a practising CA, and a general commentator are all specifically exempt.

questions.stem: A mutual fund distributor gives a client advice that is purely incidental to distributing mutual fund products and earns only commission from the AMC. What is his position on registration?

options.text: He is exempt from the requirement to register as an investment adviser
He must register because he gives any advice at all
options.misconception: Ignoring the incidental-advice exemption for distributors

options.text: He must register because he earns commission
options.misconception: Treating commission income as a trigger for registration

options.text: He must register with AMFI as an investment adviser
options.misconception: Confusing distributor registration with adviser registration

questions.explanation: A mutual fund distributor whose advice is incidental to distribution is exempt from the adviser registration requirement. Neither giving incidental advice nor earning commission triggers registration.

questions.stem: Which entity is exempt from investment adviser registration for advice given only within its own product line?

options.text: An insurance agent providing investment advice only on insurance products
An adviser managing a portfolio of securities for a fee

options.misconception: Ignoring that financial planning advice for a fee requires registration

options.misconception: Assuming stock-specific paid advice is exempt

questions.explanation: Insurance agents advising only on insurance products are exempt. Advising on a portfolio of securities, financial planning and stock-specific paid calls all fall within 'investment advice' and require registration.

concepts.title: Net Worth Requirements and Obligations of Investment Advisers
concepts.description: The regulations set capital-adequacy floors and conduct obligations for advisers. A body corporate must maintain a net worth of at least Rs. 25 lakhs, while an individual or partnership firm needs net tangible assets of at least Rs. 1 lakh; existing advisers had one year to comply. Beyond capital, advisers must disclose all conflicts of interest as they arise and must not accept any consideration except from the client in respect of the securities or products advised on.
misconceptions: Swapping the Rs. 25 lakh corporate figure with the Rs. 1 lakh individual figure
Believing an adviser may take commissions from a product manufacturer in addition to client fees
Thinking conflicts of interest need not be disclosed if immaterial

objectives.text: State the net-worth thresholds for corporate and individual investment advisers
Apply the conflict-of-interest and only-advisory-income obligations to a scenario

questions.stem: What minimum net tangible assets must an investment adviser who is an individual maintain under the regulations?

options.text: Rs. 1 lakh
Rs. 25 lakhs

options.misconception: Recalling an incorrect intermediate figure

questions.explanation: An individual or partnership-firm adviser must have net tangible assets of at least Rs. 1 lakh. The Rs. 25 lakh figure is the net-worth requirement for advisers that are body corporates.

questions.stem: An investment adviser advises a client to buy a product and, separately, receives a commission from the product's manufacturer for that same recommendation. Does this comply with the adviser's obligations?

options.text: No; an adviser must not receive consideration from anyone except the client in respect of the products advised on
Yes, as long as the client is not told about the commission
options.misconception: Believing non-disclosure legitimises third-party payment

options.text: Yes, because commissions are a normal part of advisory income
options.misconception: Treating manufacturer commission as permissible advisory income

options.text: Yes, provided the advice was technically sound
options.misconception: Assuming sound advice cures the prohibited payment

questions.explanation: An investment adviser must not receive any consideration or remuneration from anyone except the client in respect of the securities or investment products advised on. Taking a manufacturer's commission breaches this obligation, regardless of disclosure or advice quality.

questions.stem: What must an investment adviser do about conflicts of interest under the general obligations?

options.text: Disclose all conflicts of interest to the client as and when they arise
Disclose them only at the end of the financial year

options.misconception: Treating conflicts as confidential rather than disclosable

options.text: Disclose them only if the client specifically asks
options.misconception: Making disclosure contingent on a client request

questions.explanation: The adviser must disclose all conflicts of interest to the client as and when they arise. Disclosure is proactive and continuous, not deferred, hidden, or dependent on the client asking.

concepts.title: Code of Conduct and Suitability for Investment Advisers
concepts.description: The 2013 regulations set out a code of conduct binding on every investment adviser at all times, built on principles such as honesty and fairness, diligence, capabilities, gathering information about clients, and making disclosures to clients. Suitability is central: the adviser must ensure advice matches the client's risk profile, follow a documented process for selecting investments, understand the products recommended, and have a reasonable basis to believe the client can bear the related risks. Risk-profiling tools used must be fit for purpose and not too complex for the client to understand.
prerequisites: Net Worth Requirements and Obligations of Investment Advisers
misconceptions: Thinking suitability means recommending the highest-return product
Believing a complex risk tool is always better
Assuming client information may be freely shared

objectives.text: Recall the principles in the investment adviser code of conduct
Apply the suitability obligation to an advice scenario

questions.stem: An adviser recommends a high-risk product to a conservative client purely because it has delivered the highest recent returns. Which code-of-conduct obligation does this most directly breach?

options.text: Suitability: advice must be appropriate to the client's risk profile
Confidentiality of client information
options.misconception: Confusing a suitability failure with an information-secrecy breach

options.text: The capital-adequacy net-worth requirement
options.misconception: Confusing a conduct duty with a capital rule

options.text: The five-year certificate renewal rule
options.misconception: Confusing a conduct duty with a registration timeline

questions.explanation: Suitability requires that advice and related investments be appropriate to the client's risk profile, with a reasonable basis to believe the client can bear the risks. Recommending a high-risk product to a conservative client on returns alone breaches suitability, not confidentiality, capital or renewal rules.

questions.stem: Under the code of conduct, an investment adviser gathers information about a client's financial situation and objectives. How must the adviser treat that information?

options.text: Maintain its confidentiality
Share it freely with product manufacturers to get better deals
options.misconception: Treating client data as freely shareable for commercial gain

options.text: Publish it as a testimonial with the client's name
options.misconception: Assuming client information can be used for marketing

options.text: Discard it once the first advice is given
options.misconception: Believing client information need not be retained or protected

questions.explanation: The code requires the adviser to seek relevant client information and maintain its confidentiality. Sharing, publishing, or carelessly discarding it violates the duty of confidentiality.

questions.stem: When an adviser uses a questionnaire or proprietary tool for risk profiling, what does the code require of that tool?

options.text: It must be fit for purpose, with limitations identified and mitigated, and not too complex for the client to understand
It must be as complex as possible to capture every nuance
options.misconception: Assuming greater complexity always improves a risk tool

options.text: It may be any off-the-shelf tool regardless of suitability to purpose
options.misconception: Ignoring the fit-for-purpose requirement

options.text: It must be kept secret from the client
options.misconception: Assuming the client should not understand the profiling tool

questions.explanation: Risk-profiling tools must be fit for purpose, with any limitations identified and mitigated, and must not be so complex or misleading that the client cannot understand and express a fair opinion. Complexity for its own sake is discouraged.

concepts.title: SEBI: Role, Powers and Appellate Structure
concepts.description: SEBI is the regulator of the securities market. It registers and regulates market intermediaries such as stock brokers, merchant bankers, portfolio managers, depositories and mutual funds, and it prohibits fraudulent and unfair trade practices, including insider trading, which is dealing in securities using material information not available to the public. Orders of SEBI can be challenged before the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT), and SAT rulings can in turn be challenged in the Supreme Court of India.
misconceptions: Thinking a civil court hears appeals against SEBI orders
Confusing SAT with the Supreme Court as the first appeal
Believing insider trading refers to any trading by employees

objectives.text: Describe SEBI's core regulatory functions in the securities market
Identify the appellate route against a SEBI order

options.text: PFRDA

options.text: An SRO

questions.explanation: SEBI registers and regulates securities market intermediaries such as brokers, merchant bankers and portfolio managers. AMFI is an industry body, PFRDA regulates pensions, and an SRO represents a market segment under SEBI's recognition rather than registering intermediaries itself.

options.text: The Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT)
A civil court in the person's district
options.misconception: Believing ordinary civil courts hear SEBI appeals

options.text: The Supreme Court of India directly
options.misconception: Skipping SAT and going straight to the apex court

options.text: The Reserve Bank of India
options.misconception: Confusing the banking regulator with the securities appellate body

questions.explanation: A SEBI order is challenged before the Securities Appellate Tribunal, whose rulings can then be challenged in the Supreme Court. No civil court entertains such matters, and RBI has no appellate role over SEBI.

questions.stem: Which practice does SEBI specifically prohibit as detrimental to investors?

options.text: Insider trading using material information not available to the public

questions.explanation: SEBI prohibits insider trading, which is dealing in securities by persons connected with a company using material information not yet public. Ordinary employee investing, SIPs and charging advisory fees are not, in themselves, prohibited.

concepts.title: RBI: Role and Functions
concepts.description: The Reserve Bank of India administers the country's monetary policy and supervises the financial system. Its own functioning is governed by the Reserve Bank of India Act 1934, while banking is governed by the Banking Regulation Act 1949. RBI acts as the monetary authority formulating policy for price stability and credit flow, as the regulator and supervisor of the financial system protecting depositors, as the manager of foreign exchange under the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999, and as the issuer of currency and coins.
misconceptions: Thinking RBI regulates the securities market
Confusing the RBI Act 1934 with the Banking Regulation Act 1949
Believing FEMA is administered by SEBI

objectives.text: List the principal functions of the RBI
Match each RBI function to its governing statute

options.text: The Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002

questions.explanation: RBI administers the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 to facilitate external trade and develop the foreign exchange market. The RBI Act 1934 governs RBI's own functioning, the Banking Regulation Act 1949 governs banking, and PMLA 2002 addresses money laundering.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a primary function of the Reserve Bank of India?

options.text: Issuing currency and coins and formulating monetary policy
Registering investment advisers and stock brokers
options.misconception: Attributing SEBI's registration role to RBI

options.text: Regulating pension funds and the NPS
options.misconception: Attributing PFRDA's role to RBI

options.text: Controlling the terms of general insurance products
options.misconception: Attributing IRDA's role to RBI

questions.explanation: RBI issues currency and coins and formulates and monitors monetary policy for price stability. Registering advisers and brokers is SEBI's role, regulating pensions is PFRDA's, and controlling insurance terms is IRDA's.

questions.stem: Which statute governs the banking and financial sector that RBI supervises, as distinct from the Act that governs RBI's own functioning?

concepts.title: Other Regulators: IRDA, PFRDA and the Ministry of Finance
concepts.description: Besides SEBI and RBI, the financial system has specialised regulators. IRDA oversees insurance, including controlling the rates and terms offered on general insurance not covered by the Tariff Advisory Committee and regulating insurers' investments. PFRDA, under the PFRDA Act 2013, promotes old-age income security and regulates pension funds and the National Pension System, which is contribution-based and mandatory for new central government recruits except the armed forces. The Ministry of Finance oversees macroeconomic policy through departments such as the Department of Economic Affairs.
misconceptions: Confusing IRDA (insurance) with PFRDA (pensions)
Thinking the NPS is mandatory for the armed forces
Believing SEBI regulates insurance

objectives.text: Match each specialised regulator to the sector it oversees
Recall the key features of the NPS under PFRDA

options.misconception: Confusing the banking regulator with the pension regulator

questions.explanation: PFRDA regulates pension funds and the NPS under the PFRDA Act 2013 and protects subscribers' interests. IRDA handles insurance, SEBI the securities market, and RBI banking and monetary policy.

questions.explanation: IRDA controls the rates, terms and conditions offered on general insurance not covered by the Tariff Advisory Committee, and regulates insurers' investments. SEBI, PFRDA and AMFI have no such role over insurance pricing.

concepts.title: Investor Protection: KYC, PMLA, Grievance Redressal and Codes of Conduct
concepts.description: Several mechanisms protect investors and keep tainted money out of the markets. KYC, mandated by SEBI for all mutual fund investors regardless of the amount invested, requires proof of identity and address through a centralised platform. The Prevention of Money-Laundering Act 2002 requires intermediaries to record and report prescribed transactions and to keep records for ten years. Grievances are routed through channels such as SCORES for securities, IGMS for insurance, and the Banking Ombudsman scheme for banks, while codes of conduct issued by SEBI, IRDA and AMFI bar misrepresentation, exaggeration and breach of client confidentiality.
misconceptions: Thinking KYC applies only above a certain investment amount
Confusing SCORES (securities) with IGMS (insurance)
Believing PMLA records are kept for a shorter period

objectives.text: Match each grievance channel to its sector
State the KYC applicability rule and the PMLA record-retention period

questions.explanation: Insurance grievances are lodged through IGMS. SCORES handles securities-market complaints, the Banking Ombudsman handles bank complaints, and SAT is the appellate tribunal for SEBI orders, not a grievance channel.

questions.explanation: PMLA requires records to be maintained for ten years from the date of cessation of transactions between the client and the intermediary. Five years is the adviser certificate validity, three years the 54EC lock-in, and one year the capital-adequacy window.

questions.stem: For whom is KYC compliance mandatory when investing in a mutual fund scheme?

questions.explanation: KYC is mandatory for all investors, individual and non-individual, irrespective of the amount invested and whether lump sum or SIP. There is no minimum-amount threshold and it is not limited to any investor type.

caselets.scenario: Priya has just set up a practice giving investment advice to retail clients for a fee. She reads the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 to understand her obligations. As an individual adviser she wants to confirm the capital she must maintain and how her registration will work. She also employs an associate who is only a mutual fund distributor earning commission from AMCs, and she wonders whether he too must register. One client complains that Priya recommended a high-risk equity product to his elderly, risk-averse father simply because it had recently outperformed. Another asks Priya whether she may accept a commission from a product manufacturer in addition to the fee he pays her. Priya wants clear answers grounded in the regulations before she responds.

questions.stem: The firm keeps transaction records to comply with anti-money-laundering law. Under the PMLA, 2002, combining the retention rule with the reason, for how long and why are records kept?

options.text: Ten years from cessation of transactions, to enable tracing of money-laundering
Five years, matching the adviser's certificate validity
options.misconception: Confusing PMLA retention with adviser registration validity

options.text: Three years, matching a bond lock-in
options.misconception: Confusing PMLA retention with the 54EC lock-in period

options.text: One year, matching a capital-adequacy compliance window
options.misconception: Confusing PMLA retention with a capital-adequacy timeline

questions.explanation: This combines the retention period with its purpose: PMLA requires records to be kept for ten years from cessation of transactions so that transactions connected with money-laundering can be traced and reported. The other periods relate to unrelated rules.

questions.stem: Ramesh wants to know who regulates his stock-market intermediaries and where an appeal against that regulator's order goes first. What is the correct pairing?

options.text: SEBI regulates them; an appeal against a SEBI order goes first to the Securities Appellate Tribunal
RBI regulates them; an appeal goes to the Banking Ombudsman
options.misconception: Assigning securities regulation to RBI and a banking channel for appeals

options.text: SEBI regulates them; an appeal goes directly to the Supreme Court
options.misconception: Skipping SAT and going straight to the apex court

options.text: AMFI regulates them; an appeal goes to a civil court
options.misconception: Treating an industry body as regulator and civil courts as the appeal forum

questions.explanation: SEBI regulates securities market intermediaries, and an appeal against a SEBI order goes first to the Securities Appellate Tribunal, whose rulings may then be challenged in the Supreme Court. RBI regulates banking, AMFI is an industry body, and civil courts do not entertain such matters.
